content: This review is one of six that examines primary medical treatment options for individuals with chronic rhinosinusitis. Chronic rhinosinusitis is a prevalent condition characterized by inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus linings. This inflammation leads to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure, and a diminished sense of smell. The condition may present with or without nasal polyps. Intranasal corticosteroids are commonly used to reduce inflammation in the sinonasal mucosa, aiming to alleviate these symptoms. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of different types of intranasal corticosteroids in individuals with chronic rhinosinusitis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the ENT Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, with the last search performed on August 11, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a minimum follow-up period of three months. These trials compared first-generation intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., beclomethasone dipropionate, triamcinolone acetonide, flunisolide, budesonide) with second-generation corticosteroids (e.g., ciclesonide, fluticasone furoate, fluticasone propionate, mometasone furoate, betamethasone sodium phosphate), sprays versus drops, or low-dose versus high-dose corticosteroids. The review included nine RCTs with a total of 911 participants, covering four different comparisons. None of the studies assessed disease-specific health-related quality of life (HRQL), which was one of the primary outcomes of interest. 1. Fluticasone propionate versus beclomethasone dipropionate: Two small studies (56 participants with nasal polyps) evaluated disease severity and the primary adverse effect, epistaxis (nosebleeds). However, no numerical data were available, and the authors reported no significant differences between the two corticosteroids. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. 2. Fluticasone propionate versus mometasone furoate: One study (100 participants with nasal polyps) assessed disease severity using nasal symptom scores. No significant differences were reported, but again, no numerical data were provided. The quality of evidence was very low. 3. High-dose versus low-dose corticosteroids: Five studies (663 participants with nasal polyps) were included. Three studies used mometasone furoate (400 µg versus 200 µg in adults and older children, 200 µg versus 100 µg in younger children), and two studies used fluticasone propionate drops (800 µg versus 400 µg). The evidence for disease severity and nasal polyp size was of low quality, with similar results between high-dose and low-dose groups. While high-dose groups showed slightly more improvement in polyp scores, the clinical significance of these small improvements was unclear. Epistaxis was more common in the high-dose groups, with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.06 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20 to 3.54) based on moderate-quality evidence. Most studies used a broad definition of epistaxis, ranging from frank bleeding to minor streaks of blood in mucus. The severity of epistaxis was generally mild, and few patients discontinued treatment due to this side effect. 4. Aqueous nasal spray versus aerosol spray: One poorly reported study (91 participants across three treatment arms) was identified. Significant baseline differences existed between the groups, and the data were insufficient to draw meaningful conclusions. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to suggest that one type of intranasal corticosteroid is more effective than another for chronic rhinosinusitis. Similarly, there is no evidence to indicate that sprays are more effective than aerosols. No studies compared drops with sprays. While higher doses of corticosteroids may not result in significantly better symptom improvement, they are associated with an increased risk of epistaxis. This adverse effect is generally mild and may not necessitate discontinuation of treatment, but it could impact patient compliance. Lower doses appear to have similar effectiveness with fewer side effects. Further research is needed, particularly studies with robust trial designs, disease-specific HRQL outcomes, and evaluations of long-term outcomes and adverse effects.
